video_title: Bonds To Reverse Soon As Yields Approach 'Line In The Sand'? | Michael Lebowitz
gist: Michael Lebowitz of Real Investment Advice argues to host Adam Taggart that US bond yields have been driven higher by narratives (Iran/oil, deficits, AI-hyperscaler debt issuance, BoJ selling, credit downgrades) rather than fundamentals — core CPI at 2.5%, trimmed mean PCE at 2.3% and breakevens at 2.5% are all back at pre-Iran-war levels while employment growth runs at a third of trend. He frames a 5% 10-year yield as a line in the sand where institutional buyers (not the Fed) step in first, and warns that a Warsh hike a week later into a supply shock — on top of 50-75bp of market-driven tightening in mortgage, auto and corporate borrowing rates — would be a major policy mistake.

insights.claim: Bond yields are set by fundamentals over the long run — inflation and inflation expectations show a very high historical correlation with yields — but narratives can divorce yield from fundamentals for extended periods, exactly as AMC and GameStop share prices detached from company fundamentals before reverting.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Separates the tradeable short-term driver (narrative flow) from the anchor (fundamentals), telling investors to size positions for narrative duration rather than assume fundamentals reassert quickly.
insights.quote: I'm not dumb. I realize that it's the narratives that are the short-term driver of bond yields. Bond yields can go higher from here.

insights.claim: There is currently a clear divergence between bond fundamentals and bond narratives, and the fundamentals that set yields in the long run say yields are already too high.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: The core actionable call of the episode: long duration is a value position against a narrative-driven overshoot, not a momentum trade.
insights.quote: the fundamentals that that really in the long run set yields are telling you yields are already too high

insights.claim: The specific narratives pushing yields higher are oil and the Iran war, rising deficits and Treasury issuance, AI-related debt, memory chip price spikes, possible Bank of Japan Treasury selling, credit downgrades, and the absence of Fed guidance — each with some truth but each debatable.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist of which headlines to fade versus respect — the ones that resolve (Iran, tariff impulse) are temporary, the ones that persist (deficits, AI issuance) are not.

insights.claim: Large hyperscalers have begun spending beyond their free cash flow and are now tapping both debt and equity markets for AI capital, creating a crowding-out narrative in the bond market.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A structural, non-transitory source of upward yield pressure — watch hyperscaler debt issuance calendars as a direct input to long-end supply.
insights.quote: a lot of these big hyperscalers have started going beyond their free cash flow and are now hitting the debt markets and the equity markets for capital

insights.claim: Public perception of inflation is systematically overstated because people compare price levels rather than rates of change — if eggs go from $3 to $6 a dozen and then stay at $6 for a year, there is no egg inflation, despite the price being twice what it was.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Explains a persistent gap between survey inflation expectations and market breakevens, and why sentiment-driven inflation trades can stay wrong for a long time.
insights.quote: If the price of eggs goes from $3 a dozen to $6 a dozen and then stays at six for a year, there is no inflation in eggs despite the fact it's twice as much as it was a year or two ago.

insights.claim: The Bank of Japan intervention narrative may be structurally wrong, because the Treasury and Fed operate a repo program with Japan that lets it raise dollars without selling US Treasury bonds outright — but the story moves the market regardless.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A narrative to fade: Japanese intervention headlines may not produce the Treasury selling flow the market prices in.

themes.theme: Inflation data vs the hawkish pivot

insights.claim: Core CPI at 2.5%, trimmed mean PCE at 2.3% and breakeven inflation expectations at 2.5% are all sitting exactly where they were before the Iran war started — meaning inflation itself does not justify where rates are now.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: The empirical backbone of the long-duration case: the war-driven inflation impulse has not contaminated underlying inflation measures.
insights.quote: inflation itself does not warrant rates being where they are right now

insights.claim: The Dallas Fed trimmed mean has been stuck at 2.28% for four or five months and median PCE is 2.7% — and trimmed mean is the very measure Fed Chair Warsh said publicly, both at his Senate testimony and after taking the chair, that he prefers over headline PCE and CPI.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Warsh's own preferred gauge contradicts his hawkish rhetoric — an internal inconsistency that makes the hawkish pivot look like jawboning rather than a data-driven reaction.
insights.quote: when you look at the Dallas Fed mean trimmed, it's 2.28%. It's been there for four or five months

insights.claim: Warsh's Jackson Hole hawkish pivot rested on the statistic that 54% of goods showed price increases above 3%, but unweighted item counts are analytically meaningless because CPI components are weighted — the number of items is less consequential than their weight, just as Nvidia's 8% S&P 500 weight matters far more than the 499th company's.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A methodological attack on the Fed's own hawkish evidence — if the market comes to agree, the hawkish repricing in the front end unwinds.
insights.quote: the number of items is less consequential than the waiting of the items

insights.claim: Fed research itself shows much of the recent inflation impulse is due to tariffs and that this impulse is waning, making the timing of the hawkish pivot especially curious.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Provides a mechanical reason to expect inflation prints to decelerate — the catalyst that would validate the lower-yields thesis.

insights.claim: Labor market strength is unreliable: a strong employment report is contradicted by massive recent revisions, ADP does not confirm it, JOLTS does not confirm it, and the most recent data at the time of Warsh's speech showed minus 23,000 jobs.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Removes the growth justification for hiking and argues the next data revisions skew dovish — the asymmetry that would break the yield uptrend.
insights.quote: I know one month does not make a trend, especially given the revisions we've had

insights.claim: Averaging recent trends, the US economy is growing at about a third of the rate it should be, real wages are flat to negative, and if you strip out AI, economic growth has probably been flat to negative.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: The ex-AI economy is arguably already stagnant, which is the recession-adjacent case that would send yields sharply lower.
insights.quote: if you strip out AI, it's probably been flat to negative

insights.claim: A 5% 10-year Treasury yield is a line in the sand for the economy, the stock market, definitely the Treasury and possibly the Fed, and likely represents the maximum upside in yield in the short run.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Gives a specific level at which to begin scaling into duration, and a level whose breach would invalidate the thesis.
insights.quote: I do think that 10-year bond yields at 5%. Is potentially a line in the sand for both the economy, the stock market, and definitely the Treasury, and possibly the Fed.

insights.claim: The market put at 5% is more powerful than the central planner put, because insurance companies, pension funds and endowments will buy at 5% for asset-liability matching reasons — and that bid is probably already creeping in via laddering below 5%.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Reframes the yield ceiling as a private-sector ALM bid rather than a policy intervention — meaning it can arrive without any Fed action.
insights.quote: I think the market may step in at 5% before central planners.

insights.claim: Treasury Secretary Bessent has already intervened by increasing buybacks, while the Fed is a less likely backstop because Warsh has been adamant that QE is a bad thing.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Identifies the Treasury, not the Fed, as the active official backstop for the long end — watch buyback announcements rather than FOMC statements.

insights.claim: Equity weakness would be a self-reinforcing catalyst for lower yields, because money that rotated from bonds to stocks chasing 20% annual returns would rotate back once 5% risk-free looks like a no-brainer against falling equity prices.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Makes long duration a hedge that pays off precisely when equity exposure hurts — a genuine diversification argument at current yields.

insights.claim: Getting yields down quickly would require an event — absent something severely bad happening to the economy, yields will not fall fast because the narratives remain in place.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for a grind rather than a snapback, arguing against leveraged or short-dated expressions of the duration trade.
insights.quote: it would take an event to push yields down quickly

insights.claim: Trailing 10-year annualized bond returns are at generational lows comparable to the 1950s and 1861, and historically forward returns shoot up sharply from those low points — effectively the inverse of the CAPE chart for equities.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A long-horizon valuation signal that argues for structurally raising fixed income allocation from a starting point of maximum unpopularity.

insights.claim: CAPE is sitting at roughly 41, implying zero equity returns over the next 10 years, setting up a juxtaposition where equities have done really well and are poised to head lower while bonds are putting in a horrendous performance.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: The relative-value case for rotating from equities to bonds rests on two opposing valuation extremes at once.
insights.quote: Cape is sitting at like 41, implying that returns for the next 10 years are going to be zero

insights.claim: This bond drawdown is worse than prior episodes because rates were held so low for so long that there was no coupon to offset price declines — in the 1950s analogue coupons were 2.5%, not 1.5% — which also means today's near-5% coupons make the next cycle materially different.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Explains why past bond bear markets are a poor guide to forward returns from here — the carry cushion has been restored.

insights.claim: Buying a five-year bond at 5% is effectively a free option: the worst case is holding to maturity and earning 5% a year, while if yields fall to 2.5% and stocks drop 30% you sell the bond for a price profit and buy equities on sale.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: The cleanest expression of the trade for individual investors: hold-to-maturity floor plus optionality to fund an equity drawdown purchase.
insights.quote: You have that free option to sell the bond, take your price profit, and now buy stocks on sale.

insights.claim: 5% yields are already available today in good corporate names because corporates trade at a spread to Treasuries — so investors do not have to wait for the 10-year to reach 5% to access that level of income.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: An immediately actionable entry point at the stated target yield, with credit risk as the tradeoff.

insights.claim: The right entry is confirmation, not the exact low — it is better to buy the 10-year at 4.50% with high confidence it is going to 2.50% than to catch a falling knife at 5%.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A discipline rule that trades away top-ticking for a materially better risk/reward — relevant to anyone tempted to average down into the selloff.
insights.quote: I'd rather be at a point where we buy it let's just hypothetically say the tenure at 450 versus 5% but a lot more confidence that we're at 450 going to 250 versus catching a falling knife at 5%

insights.claim: The guest openly concedes the call has been wrong for the last couple of years — right for a while, then recently wrong because of Iran — and stresses that bonds require a more patient outlook than stocks.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Calibrates the track record: this is a repeatedly-early thesis, which argues for laddering in rather than a single large position.
insights.quote: we've been wrong for the last couple years. You know, right for a while, now recently wrong because of Iran.

insights.claim: The market has already effectively hiked for the Fed — auto loans, credit card rates, mortgages and corporate loans are tied to the three-to-ten-year part of the curve and have risen 50 to 75 basis points, with a 3-to-9 month lag before the tightening shows up in the economy.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Quantifies the tightening already in the pipeline — a Fed hike on top of it compounds an economic slowdown that hasn't yet appeared in data.
insights.quote: They've gone up significantly, 50 to 75 basis points. So, there has been a lot of tightening in the economy, and that can take anywhere from 3 to nine months to start showing up.

insights.claim: The Fed runs the risk of a big policy mistake if it hikes, especially multiple times, because it would be tightening into a supply shock — before the Iran war nobody thought the Fed would be raising rates, and the employment market has gotten decidedly weaker since.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: The clearest articulated risk to the growth and equity outlook — hiking into an oil-driven supply shock is the classic recession-inducing error.
insights.quote: I think he runs the risk of a big policy mistake if they hike, especially if they hike multiple times

insights.claim: The market prices roughly a two-thirds chance the Fed raises rates at the meeting a week from the recording, but the guest personally does not think Warsh will hike in September, partly because of political pressure ahead of a midterm election.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A contrarian position against a two-thirds market probability — a no-hike surprise would be the near-term catalyst for the whole duration thesis.
insights.quote: the market is saying there's a twothirds chance they raise rates

insights.claim: Doing nothing is also a yield risk: if the Fed stands pat the market may conclude Warsh is weak on inflation, and that could be precisely what takes the 10-year to 5%.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A genuinely two-sided trap: both outcomes of the meeting have a plausible path to higher yields, so position sizing should reflect event risk both ways.
insights.quote: if he comes out and they do nothing, the market may say he's being weak on inflation, and that may be what's get gets 10-year yields to 5%

insights.claim: The curve flattened after Warsh's speech — short rates up, long rates roughly flat — which indicates the market accepts his inflation-fighting credibility, and further flattening should follow as the market fully prices a hiking path.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Argues for flatteners as the expression of the hawkish scenario, since hawkish credibility pulls long yields down even as front-end rates rise.

insights.claim: If the Fed hikes this fall, it will most likely be a credibility-establishing move that sets up rate cuts in 2027 — a view the guest shares with Darius Dale, who expects a quarter-point hike and possibly another to establish hawkish bona fides.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Implies any hike-driven selloff in the front end is a buying opportunity for 2027 cuts — the tactical trade inside the hawkish scenario.

insights.claim: The hawkish internal case is Beth Hammock's — inflation is still above 2% and the Fed needs to get it to 2% — a goal the guest agrees with while warning to be careful about how it gets there.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Names the FOMC voice driving the hawkish camp — useful for reading dissents and speeches ahead of the decision.
insights.quote: they need to get it down to two, but be careful how you get it down to two

insights.claim: Warsh's refusal to give guidance is itself hurting the bond market, because the market feels rudderless without the Fed walking it on a leash.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Communication policy is now an independent driver of term premium — reduced guidance mechanically widens the range of yield outcomes.

insights.claim: The midterms are not yet being cited as a reason for higher bond yields but probably will become a narrative — a split Congress with Democrats taking the House could limit spending, which cuts both ways since dysfunction is also bad.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Flags an emerging narrative to watch before it is priced — election-driven fiscal expectations will become a term-premium input.

insights.claim: Real Investment Advice's core 60/40 portfolio currently holds roughly 10% cash alongside a 20-year bond, shorter-term bonds and mortgages — a starting position in duration rather than an empty slate waiting to buy.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Shows the manager is already long the thesis, so incremental buying is add-on rather than initiation — relevant to how aggressively they can press.

insights.claim: The triggers to add duration are technical signs the tide is turning, a shift in narrative, and more inflation data — with a 0.2% CPI print making three months in a row of relatively benign inflation and the start of a trend, while oil back in the low-to-mid 90s still pushes the other way.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A specific, checkable trigger list for scaling into bonds rather than a vague directional view.

insights.claim: The expression of the trade will not be limited to Treasuries — depending on whether short yields drop while the long end stays pinned by inflation, deficit and Fed-confidence narratives, the position could be in three-to-five-year sectors, corporate bonds or options.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Signals that the highest-conviction part of the curve is the belly if the long end stays term-premium-constrained.

insights.claim: Equity exposure is at record levels across all investor cohorts and rises with investor age, which is backwards given that older cohorts should be de-risking.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart, host
insights.so_what: Identifies a large, demographically concentrated pool of forced sellers if equities correct — and the flow that would fund the rotation back into bonds.
insights.quote: it seems to go up the older the investor cohort is, which is crazy because they should be de-risking

insights.claim: The correct wealth benchmark is the return you need to meet your goals, not the S&P 500 — if financial planning software says a 5% return gives a 98% chance of meeting goals, then locking 5% in a 30-year bond, a 10-year corporate or a 5-year corporate is the rational choice regardless of equity returns.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Reframes the bond allocation decision as goal-funding rather than return-maximizing, which is the argument that actually moves retiree allocations.

insights.claim: The psychological workaround for holding bonds through volatility is to buy the actual bond rather than a fund and commit to holding to maturity — worst case you earn 5% for five or seven years, best case you sell at a profit and rotate into other assets.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A practical implementation detail that changes the risk profile: individual bonds eliminate the mark-to-market forced-sale problem that bond funds impose.

insights.claim: The secular lower-yields thesis at Real Investment Advice is intact — yields should trend back toward the real growth rate over the next couple of years — but AI is the genuine complication because it is inflationary now via memory chip prices while eventually being both growth-positive and disinflationary.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Names the specific variable that could break an otherwise high-conviction secular bond call — timing of AI's inflation-to-disinflation crossover.
insights.quote: Does it create explosive growth? Does it does it create disinflation? And I think the answer is yes, it creates growth and yes, it creates disinflation. But when

insights.claim: Memory chip prices have spiked over roughly the last six months and Apple has raised prices as a result, making AI capex a currently inflationary force rather than a disinflationary one.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: A concrete goods-inflation channel from AI to CPI that complicates near-term disinflation prints — watch memory pricing as an inflation input.

insights.claim: The data center buildout is massive and represents a good chunk of US economic growth, which is why stripping AI out leaves growth flat to negative.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz, Real Investment Advice
insights.so_what: Makes AI capex the single point of failure for reported US growth — a capex slowdown would rapidly validate the lower-yields call.

insights.claim: AI tools are already displacing real investment-research workflow costs — the guest builds his presentation decks by iterating with Claude instead of spending two hours aligning boxes in PowerPoint, a task that in earlier eras required a dedicated graphics department and all-nighters.
insights.speaker: Michael Lebowitz and host Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A ground-level adoption datapoint from a non-tech professional services firm — the kind of diffuse productivity gain that shows up in margins before it shows up in macro data.
insights.quote: It's really like having an assistant. I go get another cup of coffee. Claude's busy working on a new PowerPoint.

top_entities: core CPI and trimmed mean PCE
